title: Zencoder is hiring engineers for Dev Ops, Integration Support and Dev Evangelism
Mixpanel is looking for a Frontend Engineer
text:
Hi HN,

I'm looking for excellent engineers to join the team at Mixpanel. We've built the most advanced analytics platform available for mobile & the web - tools that allow you to dive deep into product usage patterns, understand conversion rates, and understand user retention. Nobody else comes close to our current offering.

Here are the facts:

  * Revenue is in the millions
  * We're cash-flow positive
  * We've raised $12M from top-tier investors: YC, Max Levchin (PayPal), Sequoia, and Andreessen Horowitz
  * Example customers: BitTorrent, Path, Capcom, OkCupid, Jawbone
  * We're not interested in getting acquired. It's go big or go home.
We've built a lot of stuff with not a lot of people, but we want to move even faster..

On the engineering & product side of things:

  * We mostly write Javascript, Python, and C
  * We wrote our own datastore (thus the C) & use it to power all of our analytics infrastructure
  * We ship code many times a day
  * We care very deeply about design & user experience
We define frontend engineering differently than most companies - for us, it means everything from the API servers on down through JS and CSS. It's closer to full-stack web development than anything else.

So, you'll get to touch a bit of everything - but the biggest chunk is Javascript. We write an enormous amount of JS (it's currently 55.2% of the codebase) and it ain't your momma's JS. We've built a lot of fairly serious JS infrastructure and it's been critical to our success.

For those who like bulleted lists, Frontend Engineers at Mixpanel work on:

  * Revamping JS application architecture
  * Helping us decide on tools
  * Building out new infrastructure
  * API design & implementation
  * Building client libraries for many platforms
  * Building data visualization & reporting tools
Culturally, we have a minor case of NIH - we've built our own datastore, monitoring, documentation management, frontend framework, memcache client, and more. If something doesn't fit our needs, we're happy to build it ourselves, and we're looking for others who feel the same way.

On that note, if you:

  * Care deeply about code quality
  * Aren't afraid to build their own tools
  * Hack on stuff for fun. We love side projects.
  * Are ready to really throw yourself into something
and the above sounds interesting, please get in touch. I'd love to talk to you.

Tim Trefren (tim@mixpanel.com)

For more info, check out http://mixpanel.com/jobs

title: Mobile hackers: The future scares us, change it at Everyme
text:
One of the main reasons we created Everyme is because the future scares us. By default, when users sign up for Facebook or Google+, updates are shared publicly with the world. If you work on apps, you know that 80 or 90% of users just use the default provided to them. That means that a large percentage of people are sharing content with Googlebot and Facebook public search without knowing.

To verify that this is true, you can actually go to Facebook and search public posts for things like "doing 90" and you'll find thousands of people talking about how they're speeding on the freeway right now, amongst other illegal activities. If a simple search can reveal thousands of people sharing things that can make them un-hireable, can get them locked up, or have their insurance rates raised, imagine what insurance companies, governments, and other entities are doing with public data?

It's clear that profit can be derived from people sharing thing in public - or breaching consumer privacy - but it doesn't have to be that way. It is Everyme's mission to change the direction that things are headed in, with a combination of engineering, design, and principled decision-making that always puts user privacy first.

If that is a mission that appeals to you, join us to make the future a better place for everyone, not just users that are smart enough to change their privacy settings. Currently, we are hiring iOS and Android developers full-time in our brand new Mountain View, CA office.

Interested? Get in touch at jobs@everyme.com.

title: Hackers at HackerRank
text:
It's like inception. A hub of hackers built by hackers and we're just getting started.

Goal: To build a place where problem solvers (hackers / programmers / mathematicians, etc.) hangout to solve interesting challenges, contribute real-world problems, build hacks and many more.

Achieve: We're not trying to disrupt the recruitment industry, not trying to disrupt the education industry, etc. We are building something different. Imagine if there was a room in SF where the top 5000 problem solvers of the world came to everyday for several hours?

The value of that room is incredibly high, and its occupants would have the power to decide the pace of the world and how it should work. We're building THIS, online. It sounds like a monumental task, because it is, and it is something we're truly excited and passionate about.

Culture: We (founders) are extremely hardworking guys, and that runs into the culture of the company as well. This might sound cliche, but you have to experience it to realize the intensity of the work.

We're a small team of hackers and designers. I have no idea where each one graduated from (or whether they even did graduate). We value focused, hard work and persistence, a quality you can expect from a founder. Naturally, our hiring process is pretty tight and it requires a clean YES from everyone.

If I had a lot of money, I would invest in every team member if they started out on their own sometime in the future. This has turned out to be a great metric in building a team that you'll really enjoy working with.

Place: We're a small team based in Mountain View right opposite to the YC office.

How to apply: You can signup in the terminal at hackerrank.com, and apply using the 'apply' command (apply <URL> <why-do-you-want-to-apply>)

Come build Custora with us
text:
Hi HN,

Custora is a customer analytics tool that helps retailers earn more from happier customers.

To be a little more specific, we can point to a single retail customer and paint a meaningful portrait with his data: How much he’ll spend, how often he'll make purchases, what types of products he's inclined to buy, his predicted likelihood of returning, and more. Custora also integrates with email marketing providers and customer support systems to fuel a seamless, iterative flow of insights to actions.

From Fab.com to Etsy, some of the fastest growing and respected names in retail are using Custora on a daily basis.

Who We’re Looking For

We’re looking for a developer to join our core team. Our web stack is Ruby on Rails, and our analytics are done in R. Experience with these technologies is a plus, but we’re open to sharp developers with experience building products for the web in general.

Where We Are

Location-wise, we’re in Brooklyn, NY. We love it. Progress-wise, we’re a YC company from Winter 2011. We’ve recently been featured in the New York Times, GigaOm and BetaKit, and in the last 2 months we’ve had more signups than in the previous 10.

Day to Day

Here’s a taste of what happened last month:

Aaron implemented a Dirichlet Latent Class Multinomial to power customer archetype analysis based on customer purchasing behavior.

Martin made dramatic improvements the email marketing part of the product. He made it easier for our clients to launch multiple email tests in parallel, and added four new email providers to our growing list of integrated partners.

Jon and David worked together to completely redesign the interface of the application. We moved from an interface that focused on browsing through dashboards to one that delivers answers to specific questions.

Outside the office, Corey and Dave manned a booth at a big e-retailer conference and developed a Blackjack-style Custora game to play with prospective clients.

What We Offer

Our compensation is competitive with anyone on the market. Since you’ll be a core member of the team, meaningful equity is part of the package. We offer comprehensive health coverage, including a dental and vision package. Lunches are paid for and we usually eat as a team. We do happy hours at least twice a month and play bocce ball competitively (sort of). Our vacation policy is based on trust — take what’s needed and keep the rest of the team up to speed.

Let’s Chat

If you’re interested, apply online at http://www.custora.com/careers

title: Make the world move faster
text:
Have you ever wondered what it takes to make the entire world move faster? For instance, if something is expected to take 10 years to build, what can be done to make it to 5?

If you can acquire skills faster and companies/visionaries can find you quicker than the current timeframe (you know how long it takes to hire a developer or a designer), things automatically move faster. You definitely don't need 4 years of school to become a good programmer.

This boils down to creating a place where the entire talent of the world resides. Imagine a room where the top problem solvers hangout and they come by every single day. The value of the room is unimaginably high. The possibilities are endless - from forming a close knit community where people can learn from each other (like codecademy/treehouse?) to connecting them with the right opportunities (like interviewstreet?), solving real problems and many more. The crux being, build the world's largest talent hub.

We're starting off creating a site for programmers/problem-solvers with components and challenges that attract them to come back every single day. We've a great roadmap, a very ambitious goal and top tier investors backing us. We'll need talented folks to build a talent hub - this is like inception :)

About us: We're a small team based in Bay Area. We've had 3-4 failed ideas prior, have gone bankrupt in the past and made (make) tons of mistakes. But, we learn. Ship, measure, learn, iterate. That's how we've been living for the last 2 years and will continue to grow and move fast.

Heads-up: You'll be an early member in our startup journey. As you might know, it is not meant for everyone and the ride is really hard and strenuous. Highs are extreme highs and lows are real lows. The founders (we) are extreme workaholics and absolutely nothing matters more than building this platform.

If you're interested in talking to us, send us a mail to moveworldfaster@gmail.com with your programming profile and the biggest failure you've faced in life till now and how you overcame it.

title: Stripe is hiring Support Engineers
text:
Stripe's support team solves problems for users, and then helps figure out how to solve the general case such that they don't arise again.

Support Engineers spend most of their time interacting directly with Stripe's users through real-time chat, email, Stripe Answers and other media. Thousands of sites across the internet use Stripe to power their businesses, and our support team helps them with every aspect of that. To do this, our support engineers must understand both code and people quickly. They see through the question being asked to the actual problem a user is having.

Stripe's support team informs the direction of the Stripe product by painting a detailed picture of how Stripe is used. In order to make Stripe more frictionless to work with, spotting patterns and investigating trends in Stripe usage is an important part of the job.

Stripe's support team manages itself independently, and develops the infrastructure we use to help our users. This means finding the best tools out there or implementing our own. To date, this has included tools for for analytics on support communications, Stripe Answers, custom Twitter tools, and more.

title: Scan the world in 3D - MatterPort is hiring its first full-stack web developer
text:
Matterport (YC W12) creates a low-cost easy-to-use 3D scanner that lets you turn reality into 3D models.

We scanned Y Combinator shortly before demo day -- you can see the scanning process and the automatically generated 3D model on our demo video starting at 0:40 http://matterport.com/#video

title: Dropbox seeking iOS and Android engineers
text:
If you've been following Dropbox for a while, you know that we've always tried to keep it simple -- in reality, the stuff under the hood is pretty complicated. Sometimes creating "simple" is pretty hard. Over the past couple years, we've had a handful of brilliant minds craft the thousands of moving parts that make up Dropbox, while keeping it easy enough for your grandma to use. 50 million people around the world now rely on us to save more than 1 billion of their files every 48 hours.

Our small (just 2 engineers on iOS, 3 on Android) but mighty mobile engineering team cares deeply about providing a simple and effortless user experience. We sweat the details of our visual and interaction designs, working closely with our PMs and designers to craft our features and user flows. We're looking for engineers who care deeply about creating a great user experince.

We've got a ton of work ahead of us, and the efforts we put in over the coming months will represent a major shift in how users engage with Dropbox on mobile devices. We'll be rethinking the mobile Dropbox experience in big ways:

- Rebuilding Dropbox for mobile devices as the main use case for Dropbox

- Building out entirely new ways to experience the data in your Dropbox on mobile devices

- Make mobile Dropbox an essential part of users' collaborative workflow

- Simple, effortless sharing with users' friends and colleagues

The Mobile Team at Dropbox works on some pretty challenging technical issues to provide a simple and responsive experience to users of our iOS and Android clients. For a service like Dropbox that prides itself on seamlessly moving your (potential large and numerous) files effortlessly between devices, the constraints of mobile devices loom large -- limited bandwidth, high network latency, bad connectivity, end user cost per KB for mobile data plans, limited device memory, persistent storage, and background execution limitations, all mean making Dropbox a success on mobile devices require a different approach than we use on the desktop.

Here are a few of the technical challenges we've tackled:

- Automatically & efficiently scan and upload users' photos and videos from their devices' cameras

- Smartly pre-fetch data to heat up the cache for responsive user experience despite high latency involved in SSL connection setup on cellular data connections

- Opportunistically reduce file fidelity for a more response experience on high latency/low bandwidth connections where users often pay by the KB

Interested? Send your resume and a little info to: will+jobs@dropbox.com

title: Work at Socialcam to become the master of iOS hacks
text:
Badges in UISegmentedControl

UISegmentedControl does not support badges. Unlike UITabBar (UITabBarItem) there is no method to add a red badge with a number indicating activity. And UISegmentedControl does not accept UIViews for it's segment items, just images or titles.

So how did we add badges to our segmented controls in Socialcam? We subclassed UISegmentedControl, and added a setBadge:forSegmentAtIndex: method. This method pulls the text or image out of the segment, adds it to a temporary view, adds a badge to that view, renders it to an image and inserts the image back into the segment. Bam!

Socialcam is a W2012 YC company based in San Francisco. We are a small team of three looking to make video creation mainstream and we are hiring. To learn more email us at founders@socialcam.com.

We're a YCombinator-backed startup bringing machine to the masses, and we're looking for an engineer with ML expertise to join our cause!

We're a small team of of ex-Google and ex-Zillow engineers who previously worked on speech recognition, ads targeting, sentiment analysis, and more. In our past jobs, we’ve learned that the challenge is no longer storing the data, but sifting through it to discover interesting patterns, correlations, trends, and anomalies.

Our product is an API paired with elegant visualization tools that lets domain experts apply large-scale learning to their data. The first application of our technology is to battle fraud online. Our system uses a combination of supervised classification algorithms, anomaly detection, and good ol'-fashioned feature engineering to ferret out the bad guys, all running on top of open-source tools like Hadoop, HDFS, MongoDB, Vowpal Wabbit, and d3.js.

We're fresh out of this summer's YCombinator batch, backed by top angel investors, and have huge plans beyond fraud. Our team includes two former CTOs, the tech lead of Android voice input, and the tech lead of Google's A/B test analysis framework. We like to laugh, push each other, and keep things fresh by doing fun events with other companies in the broader San Francisco startup community.

As the fifth engineer, you'd become a pillar of the team. You should:

- thrive on responsibility and freedom

How Socialcam designs new video filters
text:
Several months ago, we added live video filters to Socialcam. Per pixel modification and capture of video in real time is hard, and takes a lot of optimization to work well on older devices pre iOS 5. The real challenge, however, was designing cool filters. My first attempt just swizzled bits in video data: interesting, but ugly. Next, I added code to apply a matrix transformation to the color-space, and came up with scripts to build contrast, brightness and hue-rotation matrices. This worked, and we shipped the first version with transforms generated with these tools. But the process was slow, required a lot of iteration, and the filters it produced just lacked pizzazz. So, for our final version, I embedded an RGB gradient image in the corner of a video clip, and wrote a script to extract a color transformation from this reference image. Now, we can give this clip to any designer or videographer, and they can have at it with whatever tools they like. They give the processed clip back to me, I extract a color transform from it, and bam, a new filter!

If you are passionate about mobile, video, or hard problems, drop us a line: founders@socialcam.com. We are a team of 3 co-founders in SF looking to hire.

We're fresh out of this summer's YCombinator batch, backed by top angel investors, and have huge plans beyond fraud. Our team includes two former CTOs, the tech lead of Android voice input, and the tech lead of Google's A/B test analysis framework. We like to laugh, push each other, and keep things fresh by doing fun events with other companies in the broader San Francisco startup community.

title: iOS development is the wild wild west
text:
Making an iOS tableview scroll well is not easy. UITableViewCell is a subclass UIView. If you create a complex tableview with UIKit, however, by adding subview hierarchies to tableview cells, scrolling grinds to a halt. To make a tableview scroll well, you have to do all the drawing in the top-level cell's drawRect method.

iOS development is less mature than web development. There is not yet a body of best practices. Fundamental improvements like drawing tableview cells in drawRect lurk behind every corner. At Socialcam, we work continually to find better ways to build our app. We’re now hiring our first engineer to work on iOS. Interested? Send us an email: founders@socialcam.com.

-Ammon, Guillaume, Michael

title: Build the next Legos: We're hiring an iOS Developer & Web Developer (YC S11)
Socialcam does not use Interface Builder - do you?
text:
We've tried it. It is nice to be able to position UI elements by hand. When we started Socialcam, we used IB for our core views. However, as we added more complex UI elements that required layout code, we started to encounter problems. Dynamic elements not in IB interacted strangely with elements managed by IB. Odd things happened when we had modified an element and an app back-ground caused the view to be reloaded. Changes we made by hand confused IB and corrupted the .xib, breaking all IB outlets and requiring manual editing of the XML to get things working again. These problems were caused by us misusing IB. I'm sure we could have avoided them. But when mixing dynamic UI with IB, there are just too many pitfalls. Now we do all layout in code, and I think we do an awesome job!

Sound interesting? Hate Interface Builder? Think we're crazy and want to teach us how to use Interface Builder correctly? Send an email: founders@socialcam.com. We're looking for an iOS dev for our first hire.

-Ammon, Guillaume, Michael

title: Interviewstreet hiring visual design engineers
text:
InterviewStreet solves technical hiring. We were doing ok holding a single, giant programming recruiting contest every 3 months, but now that we're on track to hold a CodeSprint every weekend (see bit.ly/cs2postmortem) the UX challenge is daunting. What used to be able to be relayed via personal email now has to be codified and scaled, and there are entirely new design problems that arise when you have that many CodeSprints.

We are a team of 5 based in MountainView who work relentlessly hard and funded by top-tier investors. But the more important metric to track is the growth in the number of programmers in our system (which is phenomenal btw) and customers who're using our product (Facebook, Amazon, Quora, etc.) - we've been growing rapidly in both fronts.

We're looking for the nearly mythical interaction designer that not only is able to own the entire user flow (for both programmers and companies) but also is able to inject a functionally pleasing personality to the site.

We meet companies personally and have a sense of what they expect in the product & flow. But brainstorming with a designer in this field is going to result in very high output.

Please contact [mike+ux@interviewstreet.com OR vivek+ux@interviewstreet.com] with your information and a link to your portfolio.

The InterviewStreet Story so far...

Vivek (co-founder) started out at Amazon, where he did a ton of technical interviewing. He realized that, 80% of the time, he could have just given them an automated test instead of spending 20 minutes on each candidate. Vivek wrote a web application to do just that, saving himself days of interviews every month, and InterviewStreet was born. Amazon was, and still is, customer #1.

While at YCombinator, we noticed that a lot of programming screens are largely similar, and figured that we could make a Common App, an SAT of sorts, for technical hiring. Programmers only have to solve a single set of programming problems (algorithmic challenges and real-world problems), instead of one per company that they're applying to. Thus, we created CodeSprint, which had over 5000 programmers applying for 85 companies, including Facebook, Microsoft, and Dropbox. We believe that, in addition to automated applicant screening, CodeSprint is the future of hiring.

title: What happens when video becomes an everyday tool? - Socialcam (YC W2012)
text:
Hello,

Recently at Socialcam we have seen a glimpse of what happens when you make video capture simple enough for the everyday person.

Here's a short story:

One of our users is a middle aged used car salesman in the midwest. With the tight economy he was desperate to differentiate himself from the local competition. Then he found Socialcam. It is typical for potential customers to call around to a large number of car lots to hunt for a deal. Normally, our user would take the call and try to close the potential buyer over the phone. This method had a very low conversion rate. Now when a customer calls about a car - he asks them for their email address so he can send them more information. Then he goes to the car on the lot, grabs his iPhone, and takes an in depth video - exterior, interior, pricing, etc. The number of call backs he gets with these videos is through the roof.

2 years ago this would have been almost impossible.

Today its the reality for few. What if everyone understood how useful and easy videos can be in their everyday lives?

If you interested in learning more about how we can make this a reality for all - drop us a line: founders@socialcam.com

- Michael, Ammon, Guillaume

title: Why is iPhone video sharing so Fing hard? Join Socialcam to solve this problem
text:
Hello,

For the first time ever there are over 100 million people in America with video cameras in their pockets 24/7. Yet, when you ask your friend or neighbor how to share a video from their smartphone, the most common response is "I don't know".

What's even worse is that the apps on everyone's phones (Facebook, Youtube, and Camera) make video sharing so painful. The camera app attaches unnamed 20mb videos to emails! Requiring downloads and proprietary video players in the post Youtube era is ridiculous.

title: Mixpanel - Internships. A story.
text:
In 2008, I interned at Slide, Inc. and it was one of the most valuable summers of my life. I went from being a college hacker interested in starting a company to learning the intricacies of product design and working with a team.

At Slide, Inc. we stayed up late hacking (because we wanted to), I learned about product from an awesome product manager named Adora, and Max Levchin worked closely on a product that didn't necessarily have immense amount of business value for Slide.

After my internship, I had huge takeways:

- I wanted to start a company.

- I knew grad school didn't matter out in California

- I grew a huge network at Slide who became some of my closest friends.

- Max Levchin ended up investing in our company during the recession - a time when it was hard to raise money.

Suhail

Founder @ Mixpanel, Inc.

text:

If you’re interested in helping us build an extremely valuable, sustainable payments company that consumers will actually love, please read on to see if you’re a good fit.

We want GREAT engineers

We’re primarily a Python (on Linux) shop, but love polyglots (Ruby, JavaScript, Java, C/C++, etc), and welcome engineers of all types as long as they have a knack for solving hard problems. Contact us if you:

- are a respectfully opinionated, pragmatic, and reliable individual who is self-directed and takes pride in their work

- have a strong analytical background (e.g.math, physics, computer science, electrical/computer engineering, hackers of all kind)

- have strong programming experience (i.e. you've actually coded ;))

- are comfortable with SQL and data modeling (i.e. you understand databases)

- don't reinvent the wheel, instead you leverage existing proven libraries and glue them together efficiently to accomplish your tasks

- are comfortable with contributing back to the community through open source

- get shit done. 80% solution is OK for you, but you task yourself to clean up the remaining 20% in your backlog

- are not afraid of speaking your mind, but not afraid of listening either

Bonus points if you

- are comfortable with web API design, adhering to RESTful principles

- are comfortable with OO design and adhere to the Single Responsibility Principle

- love automation, because your time is too valuable to do the same thing over and over again

- have ops/sysadmin experience, ideally with AWS

- Love unit testing, integration testing, and end to end system testing. OK, maybe you don’t love it, but you respect it

About Us

We love developers! We are a small team of developers building a product for other developers, so we take great pride in the code and documentation we produce. We hate the needless complexity that comes from technical masturbation, and always try to strike a balance between speed and quality while maintaining values of excellence. Here’s a bit more about us in bullet-point format:

- Founders were early employees at a start-up that recently had a successful exit.

- We maintain popular open source projects and contribute to open source regularly.

- We pride ourselves on healthy initiatives! We are all active runners, climbers, among many other things. We offer a free gym membership.

- We are less than 10 people and are looking for individuals who can help us solidify our company culture.

We offer benefits, competitive salaries, equity stakes, vacation time, reimbursed commuting, free wifi dongles, a stipend if you live within 1 mile of office, etc.

Our Technologies & Philosophies

- Python is used for almost everything from the web front-end, to our API, to our fraud data mining and analysis.

- Some of the tools we use and love: SQLAlchemy, Mako, Werkzeug, Fabric, Gunicorn.

- We use PostgreSQL - it is awesome.

- We love to leverage existing proven technologies like rsyslog, postfix, etc.

- We use different languages when we need to, but, we understand the relationship between cognitive load and components and how they apply to technical debt, so we adhere to "pragmatism beats purity."

- We love standards and automation. Our code base is all pep8, we pylint on every commit and we deploy to production about 20 to 25 times a day -- AS A PAYMENTS COMPANY!

We don't go down. EVER.

Contact Us

Send over a resume, or preferably, if you have any public accounts that showcases your expertise (e.g. github, stackoverflow, quora) send that over too. Feel free to highlight any significant or relevant projects you want to share with us!

text:
We're a small, well-funded startup looking for a talented visual/UI designer with the desire to grow into all areas of product and UX design.

THE OPPORTUNITY

This is your chance to join a talented and hardworking team of 5 people driven to make great products that improve people's lives. You'll spend most of your time working side-by-side with our lead designer (an Adaptive Path alum) in an end-to-end product design process doing:

   - User Research
   - Product Strategy
   - Brainstorming
   - Sketching
   - Interaction Design
   - User Testing
   - Visual/UI Design
   - Product Branding
You don't need to be an expert at all of these things – that's why you'll be working in a design pair, so you can build on each others' strengths. This is a rare opportunity: having TWO designers working together at a startup this small.

It’s a fantastic chance to craft a user experience from concept to shipping product, backed by an outstanding engineering team, deep technology, and solid business.

ABOUT YOU

First and foremost, we're looking for a talented visual/UI designer with impeccable taste who can craft beautiful mobile interfaces – someone who sweats the details and strives for Apple-quality (or better) pixel perfection.

You'll also be involved in every part of the design process, from user research and strategy to interaction design and branding. The right person for the job will see this as a big plus!

Here’s some basic stuff we’re looking for:

   - 1-3 years experience doing UI design
   - Experience designing gorgeous iPhone app UIs
   - Impeccable design taste
   - A curious nature and a desire to learn all aspects of product design
Extra points to folks with experience in:

   - Industrial design
   - Branding and logo design
   - Android app design
   - Web design
Previous work history and an extensive portfolio are a plus, but our main goal is to find someone with great taste who's willing to work hard and grow with us.

ABOUT US

We're a well-funded early-stage startup based in downtown San Francisco, working to redefine a product millions of people use every day – and make it great. (Sorry to be so vague, we're happy to share more once you get in touch with us.) We're a diverse team of 5 people consisting mostly of UC Berkeley grads. We participated in Y Combinator this summer and have been funded by some of the most respected VCs in Silicon Valley. We're working hard to launch in the next few months, and we're looking for a talented visual/UI designer to join our team and help us make a dent in the universe.

INTRIGUED? APPLY!

If you think you'd be a great addition to our team, please send your resume and portfolio to ucbstartup@gmail.com. Also, send along a few links to design work you find inspiring and a short explanation why.

We offer competitive salaries, equity and medical/dental/vision insurance. We’re happy to consider applications from folks not living in the Bay Area who are willing to relocate.

YC S11 company seeks devs to help hack online advertising
text:
We're an unannounced YC startup building a layer of web services that make it easy to run banner ad campaigns that outperform AdWords.

We've raised money from some of the best investors in the valley including a few of your heroes. Our stack runs on RoR, MongoDB, Redis, and Node. We use a lot of coffeescript. We're on pace to hit a spectacular run-rate in 6 months. We're looking for rails developers to join the team.

What we're building concerns everyone who does business on the web. It's a big deal that's worth your time and brainpower. Here's why:

In the last 3 years, a revolution has happened in display advertising (banner ads) as Madison Avenue marketers began using algorithms to buy and sell banner impressions in real-time^ and to alter the ads themselves in real-time^^ so they show the perfect message to every reader.

This combination of dynamic content and real-time ad buying lets the top brands run ad campaigns that blow AdWords away. Google knows this, which is why it bought DoubleClick a few years back^^^, and then more recently Invite Media^^^^ and now Admeld^^^^^. They're hoping to lock up display advertising like they locked up paid search.

We're building tools and services that introduce these techniques to the rest of the world. We're currently helping your favorite startups acquire users quickly and affordably. We're helping your favorite nightclubs fill up on off nights. We're helping small brands compete with the big guys.

If you want to be a part of taking digital advertising 2.0 to the masses, ping us at ads.can.be.rad@gmail.com

-----------------

^ These real-time ad buying platforms are called "DSPs" in the ad-tech world (Demand-side platform). It's a lot like HFT for online ads, with agencies programming "robots" to buy and sell inventory in milliseconds. The first DSPs came on the scene just a few years ago. Google predicts that 50% of all display ads will be bought via DSPs using algorithms by 2014. Software is taking over the ad world, too. I bet you had no idea online advertising was so interesting.

^^ Good examples of this kind of dynamic creative are those Zappos ads that show you the shoes you almost bought. Also, those Virgin America ads telling you about cheap flights from the city you're in to the city you visited last month. People are clicking the crud out of these things.

^^^ DoubleClick was the biggest player in the display space. Google bought them for $3.1b: Link: http://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/14/technology/14DoubleClick.html

title: WePay is hiring web engineers (and interns)
text:
https://www.wepay.com/jobs

A post from one of our engineers on why we are hiring:

It’s no secret WePay is growing. With more customers and more success, though, comes more responsibility. We need to divvy up some of that responsibility to new hires, as there is just too much work for this small group anymore.

We’re still asked in what areas we’re outgrowing our current team, and more specifically, “why are you hiring?” This question came up the other day, so I thought I’d share the answers here to better inform the rest of our readers what our current needs are.

Why are we hiring? Because we need help in:

* UI: As your customer base grows (along with your company’s reputation), the overall expectation of a quality product grows with it. Bugs that are a minor irritation for some people are dealbreakers for others, especially when you’re taking on an industry giant – so minor problems make you lose customers (often permanently, given the “tried them three years ago, buggy, will not come back” attitude of most people). We’re taking on PayPal – which, while not exactly known for a quality user experience, is extremely stable. We found this problem increased by at least an order of magnitude when we launched our stores product.

* Testing: Front and back-end. Like above, growth = reputation = expectation of quality. Gotta keep things stable, and there are some things that have absolutely zero margin for error (I’ve spent three days to produce a three-line patch, simply because I had to be aware of and handle dozens of different scenarios, and making an error could result in the wrong amount of money ending up in an account. Yes, it worked correctly)

* Support: If you’re dealing with people’s money, it’s kind of a big deal. I’ll let you use your imagination.

* Fraud: A non-trivial portion of our payment review involves human screening. With a couple hundred payments per day, that’s manageable. Hundreds or thousands per hour? Not so much. We have to make smarter automated rules to avoid human screening where possible, and improve the UX in our back-end review panels so that humans can make intelligent decisions faster where necessary. Good code can replace (or free up, or avoid the need for) several human reviewers, and good human reviewers are just as hard to hire as good programmers. This and support are currently our tightest bottlenecks, since they directly limit the number of payments we can process in a day.

* UX: Not so much “is it pretty?”, but “does it do what I want?”, “will I use it again?”, etc. A huge percentage of our user base is virally acquired (ex. someone who previously made a donation comes back and sets up his own donation campaign and starts collecting money), which costs us nothing. The more we can entice users to stay engaged or engage their friends, the faster we can grow. If we can turn a payment receipt into a customer acquisition medium (customer meaning person collecting money, not paying), that’s more users at effectively no cost to us.

* Scaling (in the traditional code sense): Not just server load, but weird problems that simply don’t happen except at volume – database row locking, update collisions, etc. Detecting and fixing those types of problems is much harder than most people would think.

* Sales + Marketing: Not only expanding your markets, but making sure that as you’re spending more on those efforts that your spending is effective. Have you saturated a tiny niche? You need more niches, and bigger groups to go after.

* Compliance and legal stuff: Did you know that as your annual payment volume increases, you have to adhere to stricter security guidelines for PCI compliance? While we’ve always held ourselves above and beyond the strictest guidelines, you still have to deal with compliance audits and such that don’t happen at lower payment volume.

* Analytics and metrics: We’re past the point where we can randomly guess at what’s working and what’s not. While we don’t hold ourselves up with internal red tape and politics, we do actually need to measure the efficacy of the changes we’re making. It’s no longer a single new customer bumping the graphs by 20%, so we need pretty fine-grained measurements for this kind of thing (thankfully, we have enough volume where we don’t need to let stuff sit in production for weeks to get a statistically significant sample size)

There’s plenty more than that – most is quite general, though some is very specific to our company (fraud, in particular), and obviously not all of it is specific to engineering. My day-to-day is around payment stability and related back-end services, which also includes fraud management and our admin panel. Working 50+ hour weeks – quite a bit less intense than the 80+ I did during YC, but actually sustainable – simply doesn’t allot me enough bandwidth to do everything that I need to do.

title: WePay is hiring future entrepreneurs
text:
A payments company is really like 8 businesses in one - that's why the "PayPal Mafia" is so celebrated as a team of entrepreneurs who came together to pull off the impossible.

WePay is rethinking the way payments are done - from user interface to customer service to fraud prevention - using techniques and data that have only recently come available.

We hire people who are driven, ambitious and visionary - and who want to tackle hard problems and leave a lasting mark on the world. Typically, our biggest competitor when we are trying to hire someone is an application to Y Combinator.

If you are an entrepreneur at heart, but want to learn as part of a fast growing team first - let's chat.

Here's a blog post written by our first engineer about why we need to hire more great people:

* UI: As your customer base grows (along with your company’s reputation), the overall expectation of a quality product grows with it. Bugs that are a minor irritation for some people are dealbreakers for others, especially when you’re taking on an industry giant – so minor problems make you lose customers (often permanently, given the “tried them three years ago, buggy, will not come back” attitude of most people). We’re taking on PayPal – which, while not exactly known for a quality user experience, is extremely stable. We found this problem increased by at least an order of magnitude when we launched our stores product.

* Testing: Front and back-end. Like above, growth = reputation = expectation of quality. Gotta keep things stable, and there are some things that have absolutely zero margin for error (I’ve spent three days to produce a three-line patch, simply because I had to be aware of and handle dozens of different scenarios, and making an error could result in the wrong amount of money ending up in an account. Yes, it worked correctly)

* Support: If you’re dealing with people’s money, it’s kind of a big deal. I’ll let you use your imagination.

* Fraud: A non-trivial portion of our payment review involves human screening. With a couple hundred payments per day, that’s manageable. Hundreds or thousands per hour? Not so much. We have to make smarter automated rules to avoid human screening where possible, and improve the UX in our back-end review panels so that humans can make intelligent decisions faster where necessary. Good code can replace (or free up, or avoid the need for) several human reviewers, and good human reviewers are just as hard to hire as good programmers. This and support are currently our tightest bottlenecks, since they directly limit the number of payments we can process in a day.

* UX: Not so much “is it pretty?”, but “does it do what I want?”, “will I use it again?”, etc. A huge percentage of our user base is virally acquired (ex. someone who previously made a donation comes back and sets up his own donation campaign and starts collecting money), which costs us nothing. The more we can entice users to stay engaged or engage their friends, the faster we can grow. If we can turn a payment receipt into a customer acquisition medium (customer meaning person collecting money, not paying), that’s more users at effectively no cost to us.

* Scaling (in the traditional code sense): Not just server load, but weird problems that simply don’t happen except at volume – database row locking, update collisions, etc. Detecting and fixing those types of problems is much harder than most people would think.

* Sales + Marketing: Not only expanding your markets, but making sure that as you’re spending more on those efforts that your spending is effective. Have you saturated a tiny niche? You need more niches, and bigger groups to go after.

* Compliance and legal stuff: Did you know that as your annual payment volume increases, you have to adhere to stricter security guidelines for PCI compliance? While we’ve always held ourselves above and beyond the strictest guidelines, you still have to deal with compliance audits and such that don’t happen at lower payment volume.

* Analytics and metrics: We’re past the point where we can randomly guess at what’s working and what’s not. While we don’t hold ourselves up with internal red tape and politics, we do actually need to measure the efficacy of the changes we’re making. It’s no longer a single new customer bumping the graphs by 20%, so we need pretty fine-grained measurements for this kind of thing (thankfully, we have enough volume where we don’t need to let stuff sit in production for weeks to get a statistically significant sample size)

There’s plenty more than that – most is quite general, though some is very specific to our company (fraud, in particular), and obviously not all of it is specific to engineering. My day-to-day is around payment stability and related back-end services, which also includes fraud management and our admin panel. Working 50+ hour weeks – quite a bit less intense than the 80+ I did during YC, but actually sustainable – simply doesn’t allot me enough bandwidth to do everything that I need to do.

I have to solve problems like “an API call to a credit card processor timed out, how can I resume this automatically in a way where I know we will not accidentally charge a card twice” and “what changes do I need to make to ensure that a data integrity check never fails?” while at the same time architecting data models for new features, interviewing developer candidates, refactoring old systems for reliability and future-proofing, and providing our support team tools that allow them to do their job but don’t allow them access to sensitive information (see again: PCI regulations). And I don’t even touch the front end anymore.

title: Build groundbreaking technology at MemSQL (YC W11)
text:
MemSQL is a lightning fast database that is 30x faster than MySQL. MemSQL is fully relational, durable, highly available, and distributed. Earlier this year we raised a $2.1 million seed from Tier I Investors.

For a 9-month old database company, we’re already generating revenue and have recruited engineers from Facebook, Microsoft SQL Server, Stanford, CMU, University of Waterloo, IIT, among others, and through competitions like Top Coder and ACM ICPC.

Data is expanding so fast that existing databases can't keep up. At MemSQL, you can help change that. By putting data into memory with proper data structures and access patterns, applications can use SQL at scale instead of using limited interfaces like Memcached or NoSQL.

Google, Facebook, Twitter, and Zynga have enough engineers to efficiently operate in memory, but more companies and applications will need an easy way to go into memory as they hit high traffic or migrate to the IO-bottlenecked Cloud.

We’re working to change the state of the art. We’re hiring. Join us.

Responsibilities: · Work with a small team of engineers to design and implement core database components of MemSQL · Formulate and refine new data structures, access patterns, and algorithms · Work on distributed systems architecture

Requirements: · 2+ years of systems-level experience · C/C++ mastery · Ability to understand, develop, and implement advanced data structures and algorithms

Benefits: · Pre-Series A option grant · Market salary · Cool work environment in SF (18 foot ceilings, natural lighting, cherrywood floors) · 100% coverage of medical, dental, and vision insurance · Catered breakfasts, lunches, dinners

Send your resume to yc@memsql.com

title: Engineering role opens at E la Carte (restaurant tablets, YC S10)
text:
Have you thought of what well-designed software could do if it was easily accessible in social, physical environments like restaurants?

E la Carte (www.elacarte.com) is a Silicon Valley startup out of MIT that develops tablets for restaurant tables so guests can order, play games and pay from their seats (split the bill!) without having to wait. You may already have used our product in the wild. We're funded by top VC investors, restaurant executives as well as the creators of Dropbox, Groupon, Greplin and Reddit.

Requirements

- Required language knowledge includes C++, Python, Javascript and Perl, as well as experience using SQL, XML and REST interfaces.

- Cross-platform development, machine learning, network protocols, data mining and experience working with diverse APIs are a major plus.

Software in physical environments will change the way people experience activities as routine as dining out with friends. Our custom tablets require both hardware and software design, but our development focus is on the software. We have a highly competitive hiring process and we're looking for driven software engineers to join our fast-moving, creative team.

Our technical challenges consist of scaling a robust software infrastructure that can power tablets in thousands of restaurants - something never done before. We also face the challenge of developing a simple yet powerful front-end for mediating interactions between our tablets and guest/staff. It's not easy, but it's a lot of fun.

The culture in our team is straightforward: take ownership of your projects, communicate regularly with the team and get stuff done. No big company bureaucracy - the bias is towards action and results, not popularity and politics.Flexible hours, great debates about the future of tech and lots of free dinners at restaurants for 'research'. We move fast, take risks and aim high. The best idea always wins.

To apply please send your resume and a brief cover letter to hiring@elacarte.com . If selected, we will send you an engineering technical evaluation to complete.

Mixpanel's hiring software dev interns for the summer
text:
Mixpanel is looking for summer interns. In 2008, I interned at Slide, Inc and it was one of the most valuable summers of my life. I went from college hacker interested in starting a company to learning deeply about product design and what it was like to work on a team.

That summer I was fortunate enough to work with an awesome PM, Adora (who taught me the essentials of product development) and Max Levchin. I am still not sure why Max ended up working so closely on the product we working on. Our product was new and had the least business value of all the things Slide was working on but it was still exciting. If I had to say, I think he just liked that we worked so hard on it.

At Slide, I was determined to work hard. I wanted to know if hard work paid off so I worked from 10am to 12am. It did: Slide offered me a full-time but I declined.

At the end of the summer I had huge takeaways:

- I knew I wanted to start a company. Immediately.

- I knew grad school didn't matter out in California

- I didn't realize it at the time but I grew a huge network of fellow Slide people ("Slide" mafia). Some of these people are my closest friends now.

- I learned so much about product, working with others, and how real companies "do it."

- I learned smaller things like: git, python, vim, etc.

- I could've never built Mixpanel without having been at Slide first.

If you're looking for a similar experience to my own, Mixpanel can provide this. Apply for an internship: http://mixpanel.com/internships/ or jobs@mixpanel.com

Sincerely,

Suhail Doshi

Founder

title: Nowmov (YC 2010W) - The Oracle
text:
Did you know that people spend more time watching video than they spend on all other media, combined? Yet watching online video accounts for less than a tenth of the total -- why? Because the current online video discovery experience is terrible. Bad as discovery is now, it's only going to get worse; every minute, more than a day's worth of video is uploaded to Youtube alone.

Nowmov is dedicated to solving this problem. Our current product is an endless stream videos, ordered by instantaneous popularity; we have big plans to become an automatic TV guide for online videos -- the only place people will go to find the video they want to watch.

Our founders -- all engineers -- are David, a serial entrepreneur and web expert, and two ex Apple employees: Thomas, who was responsible for Apple's H.264 implementation; and James, who built the video processing systems for the iTunes Store. We are Y-Combinator graduates (Winter 2010) and angel funded. Our seed round was lead by SV Angel.

You would be leading our personalization effort -- finding the needles in the haystack, using MATH, if necessary. Pick your technology; our backend stack is Rails, Postgres and Redis, but we're not dogmatic about it. We have hard problems, and we're more interested in getting things done than anything else.

Here are some of the questions we need your help answering:

- the majority of our users and videos are new; what can we do to minimize the cold start problem?

- is there anything specific about video that would help?

- if we had a user's social graph, how might that help in generating a personalized stream of video?

You are:

- experienced in the creation of machine learning/personalization systems;

- comfortable with teaching your coworkers stuff they don't know;

- familiar with if not expert in modern web frameworks (Django, Rails, &c.);

- unafraid of pushing your code to the live server. On a Friday afternoon.

We are:

- generous with compensation and benefits, including early-employee equity;

- flexible about work hours;

- happy to buy you whatever equipment you need to get your job done;

- working in a great loft-style office in SOMA, a block from CalTrain;

- right upstairs from the best fried chicken and coffee in San Francisco.

It'd help if:

- you've been frustrated by video discovery;

- you want to take over the world;

- we hear from you soon.

Please email us at jobs+hn@nowmov.com with an intro about yourself and a list of cool stuff you have built.

RethinkDB (YC S09) looking for a technical cofounder
text:
We're RethinkDB (YC S09). We're building a database optimized for solid-state drives and are looking for a technical cofounder to join our team.

What you get:

  - A significant equity stake.
  - Very interesting and challenging work on disruptive technology.
  - The opportunity to define a product and lead a team of people to execute your
    vision.
  - Introductions to great people: a part of our job is getting advice from extremely
    smart and successful entrepreneurs.
  - Free housing and food in sunny California, with the possibility of moving to NYC.
  - Some compensation (with room to grow).
What you have (you don't need to have all of these qualifications, but the more, the better):

  - The determination to move heaven and earth to make things happen.
  - You know C like the back of your hand.
  - An understanding of the complexities of systems software, and what it takes to
    make these systems very fast.
  - Introduction to Algorithms by Cormen and Leiserson is your trusty friend.
  - You have good mathematical intuition.
  - You're not afraid of modifying Linux kernel source code.
  - You're not afraid of modifying MySQL source code.
  - You know a functional language (like Haskell or Lisp) and understand some purely
    functional data structures.
  - Implementing software transactional memory (STM) doesn't scare you.
  - You have experience scaling a large website.
  - You understand database internals (no SQL, we promise).
  - For that matter, you think SQL is a terribly designed language.
Here is an example of the kind of work we do: http://www.rethinkdb.com/blog/2009/10/rethinking-b-tree-bloc....

This blog post has an open problem - given the numbers in the blog post, what is the optimal page size if we can cache 8GB of the B-tree in memory? Assume the cost of memory lookup is negligible, and the queries are uniformly distributed.

If you're interested, please send the solution, your resume, a list of impressive projects you've started (and completed), and a quick blurb about yourself to founders@rethinkdb.com.

text:

  $
  $curl 'http://www.polleverywhere.com/jobs/ruby_rails_engineer.txt'
## -- Wanted: Ruby Dev With Personality

Seeking a talented Rails developer to help us build new features at Poll Everywhere.

Since we're a young company, our product is constantly evolving to meet the demands of new customers which means we have a lot of new legacy code. We want a developer that is pragmatic enough to establish a sense of direction for our product architecture, but can resist the temptation to turn new feature development into intensive refactoring or re-architecture. This is a fine line between good taste and getting shit done.

Technical experience should include:

  - Previous Rails or ruby projects that you can show us
  - REST web service architecture
  - Rack Middleware
  - RSpec or proof that you like TDD
  - HTTP
  - jQuery, Prototype, JavaScript
  - Flex on Rails gets you a pat on the back
# Tell us more about:

  - Experience with OSS and/or side projects
  - Involvement in the Rails/Ruby community through meetups, projects, essays, etc
  - Previous Rails applications you've built (screenshots are good, URLs are awesome)
  - Fun, interesting, or crazy programming languages you've played around with
  - Art, music, and literature, or things that fascinate you
# We don't care about:

  - Every technology you've used since you touched a keyword 
    (like DOA web services and HP Basic)
  - Verbose resumes (shorter is better)
# Education:

We don't really care about your education. Anybody can get a college degree. What we care about is your ability to communicate, get stuff done, and work with a team. If you feel your education helps communicate those traits, tell us about it.

# Location:

We have a physical presence in Chicago, Boston, and the Bay Area but will consider remote collaboration. Its in our companies DNA to not have physical office space. Don't be afraid to get on an airplane.

# Comp:

$70K - $120K salary, determined by perceived talent Stock options Health and 401K benefits

Good luck. Don't send us a long resume.

## -- About Poll Everywhere

Poll Everywhere crafts interactive apps for audience participation at live events using mobile phones. We make popular text-to-screen applications for polls, text walls, and Keynote/PowerPoint. You'll see us used on TV, in stadiums, schools, CEO presentations, and little Chloe's kindergarten Idol talent competition (it's thrilling) - wherever an audience can text or tweet. Our customers include Google, TED, McDonalds, McKinsey, and other assorted badasses large and small (like Chloe). We scare companies that make "Audience Response Systems" or "Clicker Keypads".

We participated in Y Combinator and are a healthy, profitable, organically-grown company. We're an engineering company that knows how to market, not vice versa.

Our company works virtually, so we're looking for people who are disciplined. Witty, tasteful humor is a big part of our culture, so you should be ready to have a good time while working hard.

# Application Process

Keep applications brief; we want small resumes with relevant experience. Be prepared to defend any laundry lists of skills. Email your interest to one of:

title: Justin.tv is hiring Python Engineers [SF/SOMA]
text:
Here’s what you need to know about JTV:

- We are by many measures the largest Rails site in existence.

- We are the also largest live video site in a rapidly growing market. If you want to check them out, some of our competitors in this space are ustream.tv, livevideo.com, stickam.com, mogulus.com, live.yahoo.com and kyte.tv – more spring up almost every day to keep us on our toes.

- We are growing very quickly. Here’s a graph of our daily pageviews since last October, when we opened up JTV to anyone who wanted to broadcast: http://abstractnonsense.com/justintv-daily-pageviews-october... Our Alexa graph shows a similar story over roughly the same period of time: http://abstractnonsense.com/justintv-alexa-2-september-2008.... We have over 1.5 million registered users, and our doubling period is roughly 2.5 months.

- Not all the hard problems are solved, and not all the equity is gone. In fact we are dealing with some of the most challenging problems any of us have come across. The scale and speed of our growth force us to experiment with techniques and technologies only the very biggest websites ever need to use. Sometimes we find something other people have pioneered, and adapt it to fit JTV. Other times we’re the pioneers, inventing new scaling solutions that we haven’t seen anyone else using yet.

- We treat ourselves well. Everyone sits down to a free catered lunch together on week-days. We have a great company health plan that includes dental-care. We subsidize gym memberships and commuting costs. Our office is comfortable, naturally well-lit, and one block from SF Caltrain. You can see it here: http://www.justin.tv/officecam

- Despite treating ourselves well, we’re frugal where it counts. We’re working our way towards profitability quite quickly.

- The people here are smart, friendly and driven. We have MIT dropouts, robot-builders, and PhDs. We come from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences. You’ll find us very welcoming, and you’ll definitely learn a lot from the people around you.

Here’s what we need to know about you:

- You know a bunch of different languages, and you’re comfortable learning new ones quickly. You have strong opinions on what makes a language good, but at the end of the day you’re a pragmatist and you’ll use whatever it takes to get the job done.

- You know Linux. You wouldn’t be uncomfortable if someone suggested you spend a few hours digging around /proc to see if you can squeeze a bit more performance out of the tcp stack.

- You know how the web works, at least from HTTP to HTML. You probably need to look up the details, but you know if you needed to, you could figure out everything from cache-control headers to why something isn’t rendering properly (in Firefox at least. Only masochists know why things aren’t rendering properly in IE6).

- You are available to work in San Francisco.

If you think you're a good fit, and you're excited about JTV, please contact us (jobs@justin.tv) with your answer to one of these problems: http://www.justin.tv/problems

title: How would you like to be in charge of Google's interface? Join WebMynd (YC Winter 08)
text:
Google hasn't really changed in 10 years and we want to mix things up a little... make that a lot! The WebMynd founders believe that personalized search is the next revolution and we are going to do it right on Google's home turf.

WebMynd helps people find their personally-relevant information wherever it is online and wherever they are.     * A good degree in Computer Science, Engineering or Maths
    * High standard of personal ethics and a genuine concern for privacy and security
    * Always wanted to found a startup or have previously founded one
    * Motivated to work for founders' equity rather than a large salary
    * You learn new skills fast and apply them immediately to get things done
    * Languages: Javascript including UI libraries, C++, COM

    * Experience building web applications.
    * A strong desire to work on website with passionate users and ideas for how to improve it.

While we're growing rapidly, Justin.tv is still a small, technology focused company, built by hackers for hackers. Six of our eight person team are engineers or designers. title: Likebetter.com (YC) is looking for a cofounder - get in two floors up
